xrefs.title: Stretching out the hand

passages.en: And stretching out the hand (καὶ ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα), he touched him, saying, “I want. Be clean.” And immediately his skin disease was made clean.

passages.ref: Exodus 3:20 (LXX, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible)
passages.en: and I will stretch out my hand (Καὶ ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα lit. stretching out the hand), and smite the Egyptians with all my wonders, which I shall work among them, and after that he will send you forth.

xrefs.note: The same four Greek words. In Exodus the outstretched hand strikes Egypt with wonders; here it touches an outcast and makes him clean, the first of the wonders in Matthew 8–9.

xrefs.title: “Master”

passages.en: And look, a skin-diseased man, approaching, was bowing down to him, saying, “Master (Κύριε), if you want (θέλῃς), you are able to make me clean.”
Not everyone who says to me, “Master, master! (Κύριε κύριε)” will enter into the kingdom of the skies, but rather the one who does the desire (θέλημα) of my Father in the skies.

xrefs.note: The Sermon ends by warning that saying “Master” is not enough; what counts is the Father's desire. The first person down the mountain says “Master” and leaves it to Jesus' desire: “if you want” (θέλω, the root of θέλημα).

xrefs.title: “I am not worthy”

passages.en: And responding, the centurion said, “Master, I am not worthy (οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς) that you come in under my roof, but only speak with a word, and my boy will be healed.

For I immerse y’all in water for a change-of-direction, but the one coming after me is more strong than me, whose sandal I am not worthy (οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς) to carry. He will immerse you with the holy spirit and fire,

xrefs.note: Only two people in Matthew say these words: John the Baptist, about the one coming after him, and a Gentile centurion, about Jesus coming under his roof.

xrefs.title: Paralyzed, thrown down
xrefs.intro:
The same two words for a man who can't move: paralyzed, and thrown down (the same perfect tense of βάλλω):

  • has been thrown down (βέβληται): the centurion's boy / servant
  • lying (βεβλημένον, lit. thrown down): the paralyzed man on a mat

passages.en: and saying, “Master, my boy has been thrown down (βέβληται) in the house, paralyzed (παραλυτικός), terribly tormented.”

Just then some men brought to Him a paralytic (παραλυτικὸν) lying (βεβλημένον lit. thrown down) on a mat. When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven.”
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT

xrefs.note: Matthew is connecting these stories in your mind. Both turn on authority (8:9; 9:6) and trust (8:10; 9:2), and end with “Go” (8:13; 9:6).

xrefs.title: Healed from a distance
xrefs.intro: Matthew's stories use this healing word (ἰάομαι) for only two people: a Gentile centurion's boy / servant and a Canaanite woman's daughter.

passages.en: And responding, the centurion said, “Master, I am not worthy that you come in under my roof, but only speak with a word, and my boy will be healed (ἰαθήσεται).
“O woman,” Jesus answered, “your faith is great! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed (ἰάθη) from that very hour.
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT

xrefs.note: In both cases Jesus heals from a distance, after he praises these Gentiles' trust.

xrefs.title: Question or statement?
xrefs.intro: Fun fact: the oldest Greek manuscripts have almost no punctuation and no question marks; scribes and editors added them later. The Greek question mark (;) came into use around the 8th–9th centuries. It looks like our semicolon: σὺ ἔρχῃ πρός με; is “you would come to me?” So to this day we are not 100% sure whether Jesus asks this as a question or says it as a declarative statement. Our English Bibles are split, most print it as a statement, but others, like NIV, print it as a question. We print it as a ‘declarative question’. For example, “You want me to come to your house?” is a declaration but a question, so we call it a declarative question and punctuate with a ? symbol. Does it really matter?

passages.en: And he said to him, “I, coming (Ἐγὼ ἐλθὼν), will heal him?”
but Ioannes prevented him, saying, “I need (Ἐγὼ χρείαν ἔχω) to immersed by you, and you would come to me?! (σὺ ἔρχῃ πρός με;)”

xrefs.note: The “I” (Ἐγὼ) is emphatic, like John's surprised question when Jesus comes to him.

xrefs.title: Divorce: Jesus comes back to it
xrefs.intro: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus gives a short summary of his teaching on divorce. He comes back to it in chapter 19 and says more. The Pharisees point to Moses (Deuteronomy 24:1); Jesus goes back to creation: Genesis 1:27 and 2:24 in the Septuagint, the Greek Bible of Matthew's day.

passages.en: And I say to you that everyone who sends away his wife (ἀπολύων τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ), —except on the ground of sexual immorality (παρεκτὸς λόγου πορνείας)— he makes her a victim of adultery, and whoever marries a sent-away-woman he commits adultery (μοιχᾶται).
Then some Pharisees came and tested Him by asking, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife (ἀπολῦσαι τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ lit. send away his wife) for any reason?”
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT

passages.note:
The debate of the day was over Deuteronomy 24:1: a man may divorce his wife if “she does not find favor in his eyes, because he has found some indecency in her” (Hebrew ʿervat davar, lit. “nakedness of a matter”). The Mishnah (Gittin 9:10, written down around AD 200) records the readings:

  • School of Shammai: only for “a matter of indecency”, sexual immorality.
  • School of Hillel: for any cause at all, “even if she spoiled his dish.”
  • Rabbi Akiva (early 2nd century): “even if he found another more beautiful than she”, from “she does not find favor in his eyes.”

The Pharisees' “for any reason” is Hillel's side, put to Jesus as a test.

passages.en: 4 Jesus answered, “Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female (ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτοὺς),’ 5 and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father (καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα) and mother and be united to his wife (κολληθήσεται τῇ γυναικὶ αὐτοῦ lit. cleave to his wife), and the two will become one flesh (ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν lit. the two will be into one flesh)’? 6 So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together (ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν lit. what God yoked together), let man not separate.”
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT

passages.ref: Genesis 1:27 (LXX, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible)
passages.en: And God made man, according to the image of God he made him, male and female he made them (ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς).

passages.ref: Genesis 2:24 (LXX, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible)
passages.en: Therefore shall a man leave his father (καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα) and his mother and shall cleave to his wife (προσκολληθήσεται πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ), and they two shall be one flesh (ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν lit. the two shall be into one flesh).

passages.ref: Deuteronomy 10:20 (LXX, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible)
passages.en: Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and serve him, and shalt cleave to him (πρὸς αὐτὸν κολληθήσῃ), and shalt swear by his name.

passages.note:
“Male and female he made them” is Genesis 1:27 word for word. The Hebrew of Genesis 2:24 says only “they shall become one flesh”; “the two” (οἱ δύο) is in the Septuagint, and Jesus builds on it: the two become one, so they are “no longer two”. What God yoked together (ὃ, “what”, is the union itself) a man has no authority to pull apart.

“Cleave to his wife” (κολλάω, to glue, to cling) is the verb Moses uses for Israel's loyalty to God: “to him you shall cleave” (κολληθήσῃ, Deuteronomy 10:20). A husband holds fast to his wife the way Israel is to hold fast to the LORD. (Genesis 2:24 and many manuscripts of Matthew have προσκολληθήσεται, the same verb with προς, “toward”, in front; the oldest have the plain κολληθήσεται, exactly Deuteronomy's word.)

passages.en: 7 “Why then,” they asked, “did Moses order a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce (βιβλίον ἀποστασίου) and send her away?” 8 Jesus replied, “Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart; but it was not this way from the beginning. 9 Now I tell you that whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality (μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ), and marries another woman, commits adultery (μοιχᾶται).”
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT

passages.ref: Deuteronomy 24:1 (LXX, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible)
passages.en: And if any one should take a wife, and should dwell with her, then it shall come to pass if she should not have found favour before him, because he has found some unbecoming thing in her, that he shall write for her a bill of divorcement (βιβλίον ἀποστασίου), and give it into her hands, and he shall send her away out of his house.

passages.note:
In 5:32 Jesus' “a matter (λόγου) of sexual immorality” sounds like Shammai's wording. But here he doesn't argue from Deuteronomy at all: Moses only permitted divorce, “because of your hardness of heart”; Jesus goes back to the beginning.

Who was listening: Jewish men, most in their 20s to 40s, in marriages their families had arranged, often to a wife about ten years younger who was married in her teens and had little say. Only the husband could write a certificate of divorce, and a sent-away wife could be left with nothing.

Into that world Jesus takes away the power these men thought the Law gave them. He shuts the easy exits and puts the weight on the man: he makes her a victim of adultery. He is calling them to go the extra mile toward unity, not division.

This is wisdom, not a rule to lift out of its setting. It is not telling a woman today that she may only consider divorce if there is adultery. Wisdom names the conditions and the response; without seeing both you can't apply it to new situations. Paul does exactly that for cases Jesus didn't address, in 1 Corinthians 7.
Bonus: how the disciples heard it, and Jesus offers another way, staying unmarried, as an ideal for those who can accept it.

passages.en: <sup>10</sup> His disciples said to Him, “If this is the case between a man and his wife, <mark>it is better not to marry</mark>.” <sup>11</sup> “Not everyone can accept this word,” He replied, “but only those to whom it has been given. <sup>12</sup> For there are eunuchs who were born that way; others were made that way by men; and still others live like eunuchs <mark>for the sake of the kingdom of heaven</mark>. <mark>The one who can accept this should accept it</mark>.”
passages.sources: Berean Standard Bible (public domain) · Greek: SBLGNT
